title: The command line and PowerShell essentials
summary: Move beyond clicking and learn the core Command Prompt and PowerShell commands a helpdesk tech uses every day. By the end you can navigate the file system, check the network and run diagnostics from a terminal.
objectives: Tell the difference between Command Prompt and PowerShell, and when to use each
Navigate folders and manage files from the terminal
Run network diagnostics: ipconfig, ping and nslookup
Use PowerShell cmdlets in the Verb-Noun pattern with the pipeline
Open an elevated terminal and explain why some commands need it
Find help for any command without leaving the terminal

quiz.q: A user can't reach an internal web app. Which command shows their PC's IP address, subnet mask and default gateway?
quiz.why: ipconfig (use /all for full detail) reports the adapter's IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers — the first thing to check when connectivity fails.

quiz.q: PowerShell commands follow a consistent naming pattern. What is it?
quiz.why: PowerShell uses Verb-Noun, like Get-Process, Stop-Service or Get-ChildItem. The predictable pattern makes commands easy to guess and discover with Get-Command.

quiz.q: You want to test whether a remote host is reachable and measure round-trip time. Which command do you use?
quiz.why: ping sends ICMP echo requests and reports replies with round-trip times, confirming basic reachability between two hosts. tracert would show the path, but ping is the quick reachability test.

quiz.q: Which command flushes the local DNS resolver cache, a common fix when a site resolves to the wrong address?
quiz.why: ipconfig /flushdns clears cached DNS records so the next lookup queries the DNS server fresh. /renew and /release deal with DHCP leases, not DNS caching.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why might a command like 'sfc /scannow' fail unless you open the terminal a certain way?
quiz.answer: Because it changes protected system files, it must be run from a terminal opened 'as administrator' (elevated); a standard terminal lacks the rights and the command will fail or be denied.
quiz.why: Many repair and system commands need elevation. Right-click Terminal/Command Prompt and choose Run as administrator before running them.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does the pipe symbol ( | ) do in PowerShell?
quiz.answer: It passes the output of one command as the input to the next, letting you chain commands such as Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU.
quiz.why: PowerShell pipes objects (not just text) between cmdlets, so you can filter, sort and format results by chaining commands together.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Understanding the PowerShell pipeline

body_markdown:
## Two terminals, one keyboard

Windows ships with two command-line tools and you should know both. **Command Prompt** (cmd.exe) is the classic shell that runs traditional commands like `ipconfig` and `chkdsk`. **PowerShell** is the modern, far more powerful shell built on objects, ideal for automation. The newer **Windows Terminal** app hosts both in tabs. For most helpdesk diagnostics, either works — but PowerShell can do everything cmd can and much more.

The single most important habit: when a command repairs the system, open the terminal **as administrator**. Right-click it and choose **Run as administrator**, or press Win+X and pick the admin option.

## Getting around the file system

The basics of navigation are nearly identical in both shells:

```cmd
cd C:\Users\Sam\Documents     REM change directory
dir                            REM list contents (cmd)
mkdir reports                  REM make a folder
del oldfile.txt                REM delete a file
cls                            REM clear the screen
```

In PowerShell the same ideas use cmdlets, though friendly aliases mean `dir`, `cd` and `cls` still work:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem C:\Logs            # list folder contents
Set-Location C:\Logs            # change directory
New-Item -ItemType Directory reports
```

## Network diagnostics you'll use daily

Most "I can't connect" tickets start with three commands. First confirm the PC's own addressing:

```cmd
ipconfig /all

   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.42
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
```

Then test reachability and name resolution:

```cmd
ping 8.8.8.8
Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=14ms TTL=117

nslookup learn.microsoft.com
```

If a site resolves wrong, clear the cache with `ipconfig /flushdns`. For DHCP problems, `ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew` grabs a fresh lease.

## The PowerShell mindset: Verb-Noun and the pipeline

Every PowerShell command follows the **Verb-Noun** pattern — `Get-Process`, `Stop-Service`, `Get-ChildItem`. Once you know that, you can guess most commands. The real power is the **pipeline** (`|`), which passes the *objects* one command produces straight into the next:

```powershell
Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending

Handles  CPU(s)    Id  ProcessName
-------  ------    --  -----------
   1842  842.31  9120  chrome
    910  310.05  4477  Teams
```

That one line finds every busy process, keeps the heavy ones, and sorts them — no scripting required.

## Never get stuck: built-in help

You don't have to memorise everything. PowerShell discovers and documents itself:

```powershell
Get-Command *service*        # find commands about services
Get-Help Get-Process -Examples
```

In Command Prompt, add `/?` to most commands (e.g. `ipconfig /?`) to see their switches.

## Your task

Open Windows Terminal. In a Command Prompt tab, run `ipconfig /all` and record your IP address, default gateway and DNS server. Run `ping` against your gateway and confirm replies. Then open a PowerShell tab and run `Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5` to list your five busiest processes. Finally, use `Get-Help Get-Service -Examples` and read one example. Note in two lines what each command told you.

So before running anything that fixes the system, get yourself an elevated terminal first.

slides.title: Same ideas in PowerShell

The friendly thing is that PowerShell keeps aliases, so dir, c d and c l s still work exactly as you'd expect. You can ease in with the familiar commands and pick up the full cmdlet names over time.

Then ping tests whether a host is reachable and measures the round-trip time. And n s lookup checks that D N S is resolving names to the right addresses. slides.title: The Verb-Noun pattern
bullets: Every cmdlet is a Verb hyphen Noun.
Examples: Get-Process, Stop-Service.
Once you know it, you can guess commands.
Predictable naming makes PowerShell learnable.
slides.narration: Now the PowerShell mindset. Every command follows the Verb dash Noun pattern. Get dash Process. Stop dash Service. Get dash Child Item. Once that clicks, you can guess most commands without looking them up — if you want to get something, you probably start with Get dash. That predictable naming is what makes PowerShell so learnable compared to memorising hundreds of unrelated commands.

slides.title: The pipeline does the work
bullets: The pipe symbol passes output into the next command.
PowerShell pipes objects, not just text.
Chain Get, Where-Object and Sort-Object.
One line can filter and sort your processes.
slides.narration: The real power is the pipeline, the vertical bar symbol. It passes the output of one command straight into the next. And crucially, PowerShell pipes objects, not just plain text, so the next command understands the data fully. Here we get all processes, pipe them to Where dash Object to keep the busy ones over a hundred, then pipe that to Sort dash Object. One line finds and sorts your heaviest processes, no scripting needed.

slides.title: Never get stuck: help
bullets: Get-Command finds cmdlets by keyword.
Get-Help shows usage and examples.
In cmd, add slash question-mark for switches.

slides.narration: You don't need to memorise everything, because the terminal documents itself. Get dash Command, with a wildcard like star service star, finds every cmdlet about services. Get dash Help, with dash Examples, shows you real usage. And in Command Prompt, just add slash question-mark to almost any command — like i p config slash question-mark — to see all its switches. Learn how to find help and you're never truly stuck.
